## The recurring friction

Given a coordination `ownerId` (`su-…`, a fleet cup's `s-…` spawn id, `pus-…` for
a power-user) — or a session you *just* launched via `capability:terminal` /
`fleet:launch-on-plan` — you need one of: its **live OS pid**, its **session
directory** (to tail logs / find the socket), or its **transcript jsonl** (to
read what it actually did). People re-derive this from scratch every time,
usually starting with `pgrep` on the terminal window's pid and hitting a dead
end. There isn't one universal answer — pick the route by what you actually
have and what you need.

## Route 1: the psu-pty discovery file — the fastest, most authoritative route

Every interactive `psu` session (this includes fleet members launched via
`capability:terminal`) publishes a small self-describing JSON file the instant
it boots, keyed by its **own sanitized ownerId**:

```
~/.papercusp/psu-pty/<sanitizeKey(ownerId)>.json
~/.papercusp/psu-pty/<sanitizeKey(ownerId)>.sock
```

`sanitizeKey` (`psu-pty-discovery.ts`) is trivial — `ownerId` with anything
outside `[a-zA-Z0-9._-]` replaced by `_`, capped at 200 chars — so for a normal
`su-…`/`s-…` ownerId the filename IS the ownerId, unmodified:

```bash
cat ~/.papercusp/psu-pty/su-b3bb3287-445a-47a5-807f-436d4a721730.json
```

```json
{"ownerId":"su-...","advSessionId":"10607","pid":1471048,"ptyPid":1473197,
 "sock":"/home/.../psu-pty/su-....sock","command":"claude",
 "args":["--dangerously-skip-permissions","--system-prompt-file",
         "/home/.../launch-context/session-10607.md", "..."],
 "startedAt":1751... }
```

This gives you, directly, with **no process-tree walk at all**:

- **`pid`** — the live host process pid (`ps -p <pid>` to confirm it's alive;
  it will show up as `node-MainThread` or similar, not literally `claude` —
  Claude Code's CLI runs under Node).
- **`command`** — which CLI is hosted (`claude` | `omp` | `codex`) — you need
  this to pick the right session-dir route below.
- **`args`** — the full launch argv, including a `--resume <uuid>`-style arg
  when this is a resumed session (pins the exact transcript file — see Route 3).
- **`sock`** — the control socket the operator uses to inject a wake / force-
  interrupt (`turn:interrupt`) into this exact session.

Caveats: the file is written at boot and is **not itself proof of current
liveness** — a crashed session can leave a stale file behind (there's a
best-effort `pruneDead()` sweep, but it only runs opportunistically). Always
verify with `ps -p <pid>` or `kill -0 <pid>` before trusting it. No file at all
for an ownerId means either the session was never psu-pty-hosted (headless
spawn) or it has already ended and been pruned.

## Route 2: the process-tree walk — when you only have a terminal / window pid

If you only have a **terminal window's** pid (from `wmctrl`, a `capability:terminal`
result, or a human pointing at a window) and need the agent process inside it,
the naive `pgrep -P <terminal_pid>` **dead-ends** on this box:

> **gnome-terminal is a single-process emulator.** Every terminal window's
> actual owning process is the shared `gnome-terminal-server` — it forks the
> shell as a *reparented* child, not a direct child of the window's nominal
> pid. `pgrep -P <window_pid>` walks the wrong parent and finds nothing. (The
> same rot bit the on-desktop reaper detector — see
> `desktop-session-liveness-ancestry.mdx`.)

What actually works: **match on a cmdline marker, not on parentage.**
`capability:terminal` (and any spawn that goes through it) auto-injects
`--launched-by=<launcherOwnerId>` onto every psu launch command it didn't
already carry one for (`capability/terminal.ts`), specifically so the spawned
agent's own process is greppable and so it knows who launched it:

```bash
# Find every psu process YOU (as launcherOwnerId) spawned:
pgrep -f -- "--launched-by=$MY_OWNER_ID"

# Or find one specific fresh spawn if you already know ITS ownerId (its own
# psu-pty discovery file names it — Route 1 above is simpler once it exists,
# but this works even in the ~1s window before that file is written):
pgrep -af -- "--launched-by=$LAUNCHER_ID" | grep "<something-in-its-own-args>"
```

`-f` matches the full command line (not just argv[0]) — required, since
`--launched-by=` is deep in argv, not the binary name. This is the same
"match on cmdline marker" pattern the on-desktop ancestry fix uses (proc
ancestry there, cmdline substring here) — both exist because window/terminal
pids are not durable handles.

## Route 3: the DB route — `harness_shared.tool_invocations` / `adv_sessions`

When you have an `ownerId` and want **session id(s) + activity history**
(not necessarily a live pid — this works for ended sessions too, within
retention), query the two tables that link `ownerId` → session:

- **`harness_shared.adv_sessions`** — interactive SU / console sessions.
  `coord_owner_id` → `session_id` (what `claude --resume <id>` takes) and
  `omp_thread_id` for omp. This is the durable owner↔native-session link.
- **`harness_shared.spawned_agents`** — fleet cups. `session_owner` (the
  ownerId) → `spawn_id` + `session_id`. Also match `spawn_id = ownerId`
  directly — a cup's own ownerId often *is* its spawn id.
- **`harness_shared.tool_invocations`** — per-turn telemetry, `coord_owner_id`
  (migration 427) → `spawn_id`. `GROUP BY spawn_id` with `MIN(invoked_at)`
  pins when a fresh boot's first tool call landed (useful for "did the newly-
  launched fleet member actually start doing anything" liveness checks — a
  durable join event alone is not proof of a completed first turn).

Don't hand-write this join — **`dev:resolve_owner { ownerId }`** already does
exactly this (`resolveOwnerSessions` in `dev-data.ts`): it returns the matched
`adv_sessions`/`spawned_agents` rows (session_id, omp_thread_id, spawn_id,
plan_slug, cwd, started/ended) **and** the `tool_invocations` activity rollup
(tool_count, error_count, started_at/ended_at) per spawn, in one call.

Gotcha: `tool_invocations` retains only ~14 days and `coord_owner_id` is
**partially backfilled** — a legacy row from before migration 427 has it NULL.
Interactive-SU history doesn't need the backfill at all (resolved live from
`adv_sessions`); only fleet-cup activity older than the column's introduction
is unrecoverable this way.

## Route 4: the session-directory / transcript walk

Once you know **which CLI** hosted the session (`command` from Route 1, or
infer `claude` by default), the transcript lives at a CLI-specific path:

| CLI | Path pattern |
|---|---|
| `claude` (psu-isolated) | `~/.papercusp/session-claude/<ownerId>/projects/**/<sessionId>.jsonl` — the **directory name IS the coord ownerId** |
| `claude` (non-isolated / raw interactive) | `~/.claude/projects/**/<sessionId>.jsonl` (global, not owner-keyed) |
| `omp` | `~/.omp/agent/sessions/<munged-cwd>/<ts>_<uuid>.jsonl` |
| `codex` | `~/.codex/sessions/YYYY/MM/DD/rollout-<ts>-<uuid>.jsonl` |

If you already have a `sessionId` (from Route 1's `args` or Route 3's
`session_id`/`omp_thread_id`), go straight to the matching file — for
`omp`/`codex` this is **required**, since neither has a per-owner isolation
directory to fall back on. For `claude` with no known uuid, the **newest
`.jsonl` under the owner's isolation dir** is the live/most-recent session —
this is exactly what `resolveSelfSession()` (`self-session.ts`) does for the
`session:'self'` search sugar; reuse it (or its logic) rather than
re-implementing the walk.

```bash
# claude, psu-isolated, don't know the uuid — newest wins:
find ~/.papercusp/session-claude/<ownerId>/projects -name '*.jsonl' -printf '%T@ %p\n' | sort -rn | head -1
```

## Summary: which route for which question

| You have | You want | Route |
|---|---|---|
| ownerId | live pid, launch argv, control socket | 1 (psu-pty file) |
| a terminal/window pid only | the agent process inside it | 2 (cmdline marker grep, NOT `pgrep -P`) |
| ownerId (maybe ended) | session id(s), plan, cwd, activity history | 3 (`dev:resolve_owner`) |
| ownerId or sessionId | the transcript jsonl to read | 4 (session-dir walk, CLI-specific) |

All four are fail-soft / best-effort by design (a missing file, a NULL column,
an empty directory all just mean "try the next route" or "this session predates
that mechanism") — none of them throws on a miss, so chain them rather than
picking one and giving up.
